clue.text: Berries for those feeling peckish?

parts.note: surface reading: fruit to feed people who are a little hungry
setter's reading: wanting to give a peck, a quick kiss, as people do under a certain festive plant

explanation.walkthrough: 'Peckish' normally means slightly hungry, but here it means keen to peck, that is to kiss. The berried sprig hung at Christmas licenses a kiss beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant's white berries are hung up at Christmas, and custom says anyone standing beneath may be kissed.

clue.text: Graduate's quite missing the very thing in theatrical presentation

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts graduate, with the 's

indicators.note: missing something means lacking it, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
'it' means the very thing wanted, as in 'that's it'

explanation.surface: A graduate's not entirely engaged with the core element of a stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: A masque was a courtly entertainment of the 16th and 17th centuries with music, dance and costume, a staged spectacle.

clue.text: They instigate repositioning of limits around United

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the reordered letters go about another piece
repositioning things moves them into new places, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names

explanation.surface: Moving the boundaries around a football club like United stirs things up.
explanation.definitionFit: Stimuli are things that provoke a response, so they set reactions in motion.

clue.text: Entertainment business in Surrey unutilised, not opening unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone wrong, so the letters end up in a muddle
without its opening, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sadly, there is an unused, unopened entertainment venue in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is only a link: the fodder is Surrey plus unutilised minus its first U. Surrey is a county south-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The leisure industry is the sector supplying entertainment, sport and recreation, a commercial field of amusement.

clue.text: Say it upset rugby's foremost opponent

indicators.note: upset means overturned, which in a down clue turns the letters upside down

parts.note: e.g. means for example, as 'say' does
taken as written

indicators.note: foremost means at the very front, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of rugby

explanation.surface: A rugby player has upset the team's chief rival.
explanation.walkthrough: EG and IT together are read backwards, then R is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiger is a fierce, ruthless competitor, so the word can describe a formidable opponent.

clue.text: Oddball caught with overseas cash in Morecambe?

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so these letters go within the name

parts.note: Eric Morecambe was a much-loved British comedian, of Morecambe and Wise
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
a cent is a coin in many foreign currencies

explanation.surface: An eccentric is arrested with foreign currency in the seaside town of Morecambe.
explanation.walkthrough: Morecambe looks like the Lancashire seaside town, but the question mark points to the comedian's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: An eccentric is a person of unconventional, peculiar habits, which is what calling someone an oddball means.

clue.text: A sailor's first into the drink here?

definitions.text: A sailor's first into the drink here?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: one thing going into another means it is placed inside it

parts.note: a common drink
first letter of sailor

explanation.surface: Out on the ocean, a sailor is the first to fall overboard.
explanation.walkthrough: S sits inside TEA after A. Read whole, the clue also describes where a sailor ends up in 'the drink', slang for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the open ocean, away from land, is exactly where a seaman who goes overboard finds himself.

clue.text: Group of trainee pilots fails, coming about fourth, but not far off

parts.note: ATC is the Air Training Corps, a British youth organisation for would-be airmen

indicators.note: to come about something is to go round it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: to lose is to fail
a quarter is one fourth

explanation.surface: A squad of trainee aviators fail, finishing fourth, yet they came close.
explanation.definitionFit: At close quarters means very near, in direct proximity, so the phrase means not distant.

clue.text: Very affectionate, but denying love? What are you doing?

indicators.note: to deny something is to refuse it a place, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: 'so loving' is very affectionate
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Someone very affectionate who will not admit to love is asked what they are up to.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks to the reader: what you are doing right now is working out this crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: The question addresses the crossword reader, whose current activity is working out the answers to clues.

clue.text: Friend, invested in gold reserves, gutted — they'll get no payment

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
a mate is a friend

indicators.note: a gutted word has its insides removed, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: first and last letters of reserves

explanation.surface: A friend who put money into gold reserves is devastated, since they will see no return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' looks like British slang for upset, but it strips the inside from reserves.
explanation.definitionFit: Amateurs take part in sport or art for love rather than money, so they receive no fee.

clue.text: Happy son, working on farm, perhaps giving heart away

indicators.note: to give away the heart is to lose the central letter of the word

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
milking cows is typical farm work

explanation.surface: A son who works on the farm seems content, perhaps because he is generous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart' here is the single central letter of an odd-length word; 'perhaps' marks the farm work as one example among several.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone smiling shows outward signs of being cheerful, so the adjective matches happy.

clue.text: Company mostly contemptible, concealing large element from auditor

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hide it within, so one piece wraps another
mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
cheap can mean despicable or contemptible
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A thoroughly despicable firm is hiding a big piece of evidence from the accountant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like an accountant, but here it means a listener; CHEAP shortened to CHEA hides L.
explanation.definitionFit: The cochlea is the spiral part of the inner ear, so it is a component of a hearer's anatomy.

clue.text: Rock feature? University repeatedly collecting both sides separately

indicators.note: to collect things is to gather them in, so the repeated letters hold others between them
separately says the two sides are not kept together but each goes into its own gap

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university, used three times
L and R are left and right

explanation.surface: A university's geology department keeps gathering samples from both sides of a rock formation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Separately' tells you L and R go into different gaps between the U's rather than together.
explanation.definitionFit: Uluru, also called Ayers Rock, is the vast sandstone monolith in central Australia, a landmark rock.

clue.text: Make arbitrary change to disarm one

indicators.note: to change the letters is to alter their order into something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to make a random adjustment so as to disarm someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'disarm one' is the fodder; 'to' is a link word, despite looking part of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To randomise is to make choices by chance, so the outcome becomes arbitrary rather than planned.

clue.text: Composer regards lad with wire suspiciously

indicators.note: acting suspiciously suggests something odd or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A composer eyes a young man carrying a wire in a shifty way, like a spy thriller.
explanation.definitionFit: Elgar, knighted in 1904, wrote the Enigma Variations and Pomp and Circumstance marches, a celebrated English composer.

clue.text: Not the right infantry for ambush?

parts.note: not right is wrong
foot soldiers are the infantry

explanation.surface: A military question: were these the wrong foot soldiers to lay an ambush?
explanation.definitionFit: To wrong-foot someone is to catch them off guard, much as an ambush takes victims by surprise.

clue.text: Charge to go in weapons, as much as people can carry?

definitions.text: as much as people can carry

indicators.note: going in means being placed inside, so this piece sits within another

parts.note: arms are weapons
to charge a gun is to load it

explanation.surface: An ammunition charge is put into guns, as much as soldiers can lug about.
explanation.definitionFit: An armload is the quantity a person can hold in their arms, so armloads are amounts people can carry.

clue.text: Boy Wonder, boy on course possibly for lead role in story

parts.note: Robin, Batman's sidekick, is called the Boy Wonder

indicators.note: possibly signals one of several arrangements, so the letters may be reordered

parts.note: a son is a boy
taken as written

explanation.surface: Batman's sidekick and a lad on a drama course might be cast as the star of a story.
explanation.definitionFit: Robinson Crusoe is the castaway hero and title character of Defoe's novel, its principal figure.

clue.text: Get rid of dreadful piano, out of tune

parts.note: bum is British slang for bad or worthless
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
an off note is out of tune

explanation.surface: A plea to dispose of a terrible piano that will not play in tune.
explanation.definitionFit: To bump off is slang for murder, a brutal way of disposing of someone.

clue.text: Disputed territory, a site so in disarray

indicators.note: in disarray means in a mess, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A contested region, a location left in chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: Ossetia, in the Caucasus, is split between Russia and Georgia, and South Ossetia's status is contested.

clue.text: Indescribable pursuit in part of London in the past

indicators.note: in the Cockney speech of London's East End the initial H is dropped

parts.note: a hunt is a pursuit
old means belonging to the past

explanation.surface: An unspeakable chase took place in a corner of London long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys, from London's East End, famously drop their aitches, so HUNT becomes 'UNT.
explanation.definitionFit: Untold means too great to be expressed or counted, as in untold riches, so beyond description.

clue.text: One encouraging member to get cheese

parts.note: an arm or leg is a member of the body
someone who urges others on

explanation.surface: Someone is persuading a club member to pick up some cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in reverse order in the clue: the member comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Limburger is a strong-smelling soft Belgian cheese, named after the Limburg region.

clue.text: New recording? Rock group has nine

parts.note: R.E.M. was an American rock band
IX is nine in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A rock band has nine songs on its new album.
explanation.definitionFit: A remix is a fresh version of a track made by altering the mix of an existing recording.

clue.text: Give up, releasing good versatile material

indicators.note: to release something is to let it go, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: to resign is to give up a post
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone quits, freeing a good all-purpose substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Resin, natural or synthetic, is used for varnishes, plastics and adhesives, so it is a material of many uses.

clue.text: Going to cut energy source after conflict intervenes

indicators.note: something that intervenes comes between, so it sits inside the other piece
to cut a word is to trim off its final letter

parts.note: the atom is the source of nuclear energy
a bout is a fight or contest

explanation.surface: Power supplies are about to be cut once war breaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Energy source' suggests a power station, but in crosswords the atom is a stock source of energy; the fight goes inside the shortened word.
explanation.definitionFit: 'About to' means on the point of doing something, the same future sense as 'going to'.

clue.text: Who'll do something innovative with some art?

definitions.text: Who'll do something innovative with some art?

indicators.note: doing something innovative with material means reshaping it into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about which artist will bring fresh ideas to a piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a master artist is exactly someone who innovates with art.
explanation.definitionFit: A maestro is a distinguished master of an art, especially music, the kind of figure who breaks new ground.

clue.text: Milksop frequently observed in second year

indicators.note: something observed in a place is seen inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
oft is an old word for often
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A weakling who was often seen during their second year at school.
explanation.definitionFit: A milksop is a feeble, timid person, which is what calling someone a softy implies.

clue.text: Strain is little seen around new spot for prospective travellers

indicators.note: something seen around another thing encloses it, so the letters wrap about one more

parts.note: to tax is to put a strain on
taken as written
a tad is a little bit
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A small amount of stress is felt around a fresh holiday destination for would-be tourists.
explanation.definitionFit: A taxi stand, or rank, is a place where people wanting a cab go to wait for one.
